title: Approach to a suspected drug eruption
summary: How to work out whether a rash is drug-induced: the drug timeline, morphology, severity markers (SCARs), which drug to stop, documenting allergy properly and reporting on the Yellow Card scheme.

glance.think: Any new rash in someone who started, changed or restarted a medicine in the last 8 weeks.
glance.engine: Immune reactions (type I to IV) or non-immune effects (phototoxicity, deposition, pharmacology) of a drug or its metabolites.
glance.backbone: Build a drug timeline, name the morphology, check for SCAR red flags, stop the most likely culprit, record the reaction precisely (NICE CG183) and report.
glance.never_miss: SJS/TEN, DRESS, AGEP, anaphylaxis and angioedema; vasculitis with organ involvement.

what: Cutaneous ADRs affect ~2–3% of hospital inpatients. Most (~90%) are benign **exanthems, urticaria or FDE**. About **2% are SCARs** (SJS/TEN, DRESS, AGEP), which are potentially fatal. Antibiotics (aminopenicillins, sulfonamides), anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine), allopurinol, NSAIDs (oxicams) and contrast media dominate the culprit lists.

list: **Immune-mediated (Gell & Coombs, revised):** **Type I** (IgE): urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis; minutes to hours; Type II: drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia/pemphigus; Type III (immune complex): serum-sickness-like reaction, vasculitis (the [vasculitis](condition:cutaneous-vasculitis-approach) notes); **Type IV** (T-cell, delayed), subdivided:; IVa (Th1) — eczematous; **IVb** (Th2/eosinophils) — **DRESS**, maculopapular; **IVc** (cytotoxic CD8 T cells, granulysin) — **SJS/TEN, FDE**; **IVd** (neutrophils, IL-8) — **AGEP**

**Non-immune:** pharmacological (bradykinin — ACE-i angioedema; COX-1 inhibition — NSAID urticaria/angioedema); **phototoxicity**; direct mast-cell activation (opioids, vancomycin "red man" — MRGPRX2); deposition (amiodarone, minocycline pigmentation); overdose/cumulative toxicity

**Host factors:** HLA alleles (see *Stevens–Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis*), viral infection (EBV + amoxicillin; HIV ↑ sulfonamide reactions; HHV-6 reactivation in DRESS), older age, renal impairment, autoimmune disease.

ol: **Drug chart/timeline**. List every drug, with start/stop/dose-change dates, for the previous **8 weeks** (up to 3 months for DRESS). Include **OTC, herbal, supplements, recreational drugs, contrast, vaccines and depot/long-acting drugs**. Plot the rash onset against each one. A drug started >8 weeks before the rash (and taken without problem) is less likely; one started after onset can be excluded.
**Previous exposure:** a previous reaction to the same or a cross-reacting drug; re-exposure shortens the latency.
**Morphology and extent:** pattern (above), **mucosal involvement**, skin pain, Nikolsky sign, blisters/detachment (% BSA), pustules, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, purpura.

**Investigations:** **FBC with differential** (eosinophilia → DRESS; lymphopenia → SJS/TEN; atypical lymphocytes; neutrophilia → AGEP); U&E and LFTs (DRESS hepatitis/nephritis); CRP, glucose and bicarbonate (SCORTEN); Urinalysis (vasculitis); CK; TFTs (DRESS late effect); Viral serology/PCR (EBV, HHV-6, *Mycoplasma* in EM/SJS-like mucositis); **Skin biopsy** (H&E ± direct immunofluorescence — confirms SJS/TEN, AGEP, vasculitis; excludes AIBD/SSSS); **Mast-cell tryptase** within 1–4 h of suspected anaphylaxis; Later, by the **allergy service**: skin prick/intradermal tests, patch tests (FDE lesional patch, DRESS/AGEP delayed patch), lymphocyte transformation tests, and oral **drug provocation** for low-risk penicillin allergy. **Never rechallenge after SJS/TEN or DRESS.**

**Causality tools:** **Naranjo** — a general ADR probability scale (10 questions; ≥9 definite, 5–8 probable, 1–4 possible, ≤0 doubtful); **ALDEN** — specific to SJS/TEN (see *Stevens–Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis*); **RegiSCAR** — DRESS scoring

differentials: Viral exanthem (EBV, parvovirus, measles, COVID-19), *Mycoplasma*-associated mucositis (RIME), graft-versus-host disease, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS — superficial split, children/renal failure), autoimmune bullous disease, Kawasaki disease, scarlet fever, toxic shock syndrome, acute cutaneous lupus, pustular psoriasis (vs AGEP), cellulitis (vs FDE/EN).

list: **Stop the probable culprit** (and any non-essential drugs). Choose a structurally unrelated alternative (e.g. levetiracetam rather than another aromatic anticonvulsant).

**Benign exanthem:** emollient, moderate–potent topical steroid, sedating or non-sedating antihistamine for itch. The rash may worsen for 1–3 days after stopping, then fades with desquamation over 1–2 weeks.

**Record the reaction** (NICE CG183 *Drug allergy*): drug name, reaction description, date, severity, and whether it is an allergy or an intolerance. **Tell the patient in writing**, and make sure the record is shared (GP record, hospital discharge letter, community pharmacy PMR).

**Report via the MHRA Yellow Card scheme** (https://yellowcard.mhra.gov.uk): all suspected serious reactions; any reaction to ▼ black triangle drugs; and any reaction in children. SJS/TEN, DRESS and AGEP should always be reported.

**Penicillin allergy de-labelling:** ~90% of labels are inaccurate. Refer suitable patients to allergy or local de-labelling pathways (BSACI 2022). A "rash on amoxicillin during glandular fever" is not true allergy.

management: Mucosal involvement (≥2 sites); skin pain or burning; dusky/targetoid lesions or blisters; **Nikolsky sign**; **fever**; **facial oedema**; lymphadenopathy; abnormal LFTs/renal function; eosinophilia; widespread pustules; signs of anaphylaxis (call 999, IM adrenaline 500 micrograms in adults).

IPs can stop and substitute drugs, treat benign exanthems/urticaria symptomatically, document allergies and submit Yellow Cards. SCARs need emergency admission (dermatology/burns/ITU). Allergy testing and drug provocation are specialist.

There is no single answer. Strong answers covered: **timing** relative to a new drug, **morphology** (pattern recognition, see *Approach to a suspected drug eruption*), **resolution on withdrawal**, recurrence on re-exposure, **skin of colour** (erythema looks violaceous/grey, and PIH dominates), and patient education (name the drug, avoid it, carry an alert, read OTC labels).

management.h: Case 2: 76-year-old woman on a medical ward, multiple drugs

list: **History:** a **dated drug chart** for 8 weeks: new drugs, dose changes, OTC/herbal, contrast, IV antibiotics, and drugs given in other settings (ED, theatre); previous drug reactions and tolerance; onset and evolution of the rash; itch vs pain, fever, mucosal/eye symptoms; viral illness; renal/hepatic function (drug accumulation)

**Examination:** morphology and distribution (urticarial / morbilliform / photo-distributed / blistering / pustular / purpuric), mucosae, % BSA, Nikolsky sign, facial oedema, lymph nodes, temperature, organ signs.

**Investigations:** FBC + differential (eosinophils, lymphocytes, neutrophils), U&E, LFT, CRP, urinalysis, ± tryptase, viral PCR, **skin biopsy (H&E + DIF)**. Score causality with **Naranjo** (general) or **ALDEN** (SJS/TEN). Later testing by the **allergy service** (patch tests, specific IgE, provocation).

**Likely candidates (typical inpatient drugs):** **Urticarial:** β-lactam antibiotics, NSAIDs/aspirin, opioids (morphine, codeine — pseudo-allergic), contrast media, vancomycin, ACE-i (angioedema); **Photosensitive:** thiazides/loop diuretics (pseudoporphyria — furosemide), amiodarone, doxycycline, quinolones (ciprofloxacin), NSAIDs, phenothiazines, PPIs (SCLE); **Blistering:** in an older patient think **drug-induced bullous pemphigoid** (gliptins, loop diuretics, spironolactone, PD-1 inhibitors), **SJS/TEN** (allopurinol, anticonvulsants, co-trimoxazole, oxicams), **FDE/GBFDE**, pseudoporphyria (furosemide, naproxen) and linear IgA disease (**vancomycin**)

management.h: Case 2: EM vs SJS vs TEN

management: See the table in and the classification in *Stevens–Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis*:

list: **EM:** HSV-triggered, typical targets, acral, mild mucosa, good prognosis; treat HSV (aciclovir prophylaxis if recurrent).
**SJS (<10%) / overlap / TEN (>30%):** drug-induced CD8/granulysin necrosis, atypical targets, severe mucositis. Stop the drug, admit, supportive care, ± ciclosporin/IVIg.

**[Case 1](condition:drug-eruption-approach):** **ACE-inhibitor (ramipril)-induced, bradykinin-mediated angioedema**, possibly triggered by minor surgery. No useful response to antihistamine or steroid. **Investigations:** clinical; C4/C1-INH if atypical, tryptase if anaphylaxis is possible. **Management:** airway assessment, stop ramipril permanently (class allergy), consider an ARB with caution or a CCB, avoid gliptins/sacubitril, Yellow Card, explain that recurrences can happen for weeks (see *ACE-inhibitor (bradykinin-mediated) angioedema*).

**[Case 2](condition:drug-eruption-approach):** **erythema nodosum**, most likely **COC-induced**. Exclude infection (strep), sarcoid/TB (CXR), IBD and pregnancy, and **exclude DVT/thrombophlebitis** given the unilateral leg + COC + tranexamic acid; cellulitis is a valid differential. **Treat:** stop the COC (alternative contraception/cycle control), rest, elevation, NSAID analgesia; review; biopsy if atypical (see *Drug-induced erythema nodosum*).

**[Case 3](condition:drug-eruption-approach):** **Question 1** — main causes of photosensitivity (see *Drug-induced pigmentation — amiodarone*); **Question 2** — the visible abnormality is **blue-grey (slate) pigmentation of sun-exposed facial skin** ± phototoxic erythema; **Question 3** — **amiodarone-induced phototoxicity and pigmentation** (UVA-absorbing drug → ROS; lipofuscin-like drug–lipid deposits in dermal macrophages; long half-life); **Question 4** — cardiology liaison (dose reduction/alternative), strict UVA photoprotection, monitoring (TFT/LFT/eyes/lung), counselling that the pigment fades slowly, Yellow Card (see *Drug-induced pigmentation — amiodarone*); *(A student answer labelled this as "Q2"; it answers [Case 3](condition:drug-eruption-approach).)*

**[Case 1](condition:drug-eruption-approach):** **drug-induced photosensitivity (phototoxic) from bendroflumethiazide**. Investigate clinically ± ANA/Ro (SCLE — omeprazole), porphyrins if blistering; phototesting/photopatch rarely. **Treat:** stop the thiazide → amlodipine; topical steroid, emollient, antihistamine; strict photoprotection and education; review diabetes (HbA1c 78) and the PPI indication (see *Drug-induced photosensitivity — thiazide case*).

**[Case 2](condition:drug-eruption-approach):** **fixed drug eruption from diclofenac** (taken during two consecutive periods), misdiagnosed as a cold sore. Stop/avoid diclofenac (± related NSAIDs), alternative dysmenorrhoea treatment, topical steroid, document and report (see *Fixed drug eruption*).

**QA = TEN** (>30% detachment + severe mucositis + systemic illness). course follow-up "does TEN involve >10%?" — >10% is the SCORTEN item and the lower bound for overlap. **TEN is >30%**; SJS <10%; overlap 10–30%.
**QB = 5–28 days** (typical latency from starting the culprit; the ALDEN "suggestive" window). BAD quotes 4–28 days.

list: **SCORTEN from the data given:** age ≥40 (+1) and BSA >10% (+1) = **at least 2 (≥12% predicted mortality)**. HR, urea, glucose and bicarbonate are needed, and the WCC of 16 and ALT of 150 suggest systemic involvement. Recalculate within 24 h and on day 3.
**Supporting results:** **lymphopenia (0.3)** is typical of SJS/TEN; **normal eosinophils** argue against DRESS; raised ALT occurs in TEN; anaemia (110).

**Management:** Stop carbamazepine (and the non-essential ibuprofen/flucloxacillin unless infection is proven); Switch to a **non-aromatic anticonvulsant** (e.g. **levetiracetam**, or valproate if appropriate — **not** phenytoin/oxcarbazepine/phenobarbital/lamotrigine, all of which cross-react or carry high risk); Transfer to a burns/ITU centre; ophthalmology within 24 h; supportive care; ± ciclosporin/IVIg; HLA-B*15:02 / A*31:01 if of relevant ancestry (for family counselling); **Yellow Card**; lifelong alert

red_flags: Skin pain, blisters, skin detachment or mucosal erosions: possible **SJS/TEN**, stop the drug and admit the same day.
Fever, facial swelling, lymph nodes and abnormal bloods 2–8 weeks after a new drug: possible **DRESS**.
Swelling of lips, tongue or throat, or breathing difficulty: **999**.
pearls: "**Any rash on any drug** — take a dated drug history, then think SCAR red flags."

Give the patient the **drug name, the reaction and the date** in writing; advise wearing a medical alert if severe; check OTC products (ibuprofen) and combination products contain none of the culprit.
Write the reaction, not just "allergy", in the record (e.g. "amoxicillin — maculopapular rash day 7, 2026, no mucosal involvement").

rows: course explanation: SJS <10%, TEN >30%. Some student answers said "TEN >10%"
Agrees with BAD 2016 / Bastuji-Garin: SJS <10%, **overlap 10–30%**, TEN >30%. ">10%" is the SCORTEN item, not the TEN definition
BAD 2016 says **4–28 days**; ALDEN "suggestive" 5–28 days — both acceptable
UK: Naranjo is generic; for SJS/TEN use **ALDEN** (BAD 2016). Allergy-service involvement per **NICE CG183**. Add **Yellow Card** reporting (not emphasised in the course)
Student answers mentioned topical steroids/antihistamines for a TEN case

UK: **same-day admission to a burns/ITU or specialist dermatology centre**, supportive care, ophthalmology within 24 h; systemic immunomodulation (ciclosporin/IVIg) is a specialist decision; topical steroids/antihistamines alone are not management
MHRA/BNF/SmPC: **HLA-B*15:02 testing before carbamazepine** in Han Chinese/Thai/SE Asian ancestry; allopurinol low-start/titrate (HLA-B*58:01)
Course case and student answers: stop ACE-i; ARB alternative
Agrees; UK adds airway-first triage (999), **class reaction — avoid all ACE-i**, ARB **with caution** (low recurrence risk), avoid **sacubitril/valsartan and gliptins**; C4/C1-INH only if atypical
Course teaching: drug-induced EN (COC); DDx cellulitis
Agrees; UK practice would also **exclude DVT/superficial thrombophlebitis** (unilateral, COC + tranexamic acid) and do a CXR/ASO, and notes the caution about combining TXA with a COC
Course teaching: phototoxic commoner; biopsy/photopatch rarely
Agrees; UK extras: **omeprazole/thiazide SCLE** DDx (check Ro), **HCTZ NMSC MHRA 2018**, choose a non-photosensitising replacement (amlodipine rather than indapamide)
Agrees; UK adds documentation of the NSAID class risk, OTC checks, paracetamol/hormonal alternatives for dysmenorrhoea, Yellow Card
UK: **don't stop without cardiology**; photoprotection for months after stopping (BNF); routine TFT/LFT monitoring
